To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
macroautophagy and intracellular trafficking are controlled by the same G protein (G(i3)) and that the macroautophagy is independent of the Golgi complex.

the trimeric Go(i3) protein is involved in the regulation of the lysosomal degradation of N-linked glycopeptides in HT-29 human colon carcinoma cells; this degradation occurs via a dual control, involving both the autophagic and the exocytic pathways; the trimeric Gi3 protein is involved in two distinct membrane flow processes, namely the autophagic process and the intracellular trafficking along the exocytic pathway.
macroautophagy and intracellular trafficking are both controlled by the G alpha(i) protein in HT29 cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanism of the trimeric Gi3 protein-dependent macroautophagic and intracellular trafficking pathways of N-linked glycosylation.
the molecular mechanisms of the lysosomal-autopahgic pathway, which is responsible for the turnover of a large pool of N-linked glycans in HT-29 human colon cancer cells.
the identification of the intracellular pathways that control the degradation of N-linked glycans.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the trimeric Go(i3) protein is responsible for the dual regulation of macroautophagy and intracellular trafficking in HT-29 cell.
the G alpha(i) protein controls the trafficking of a pool of glycoproteins to the lysosomal-autophasic pathway, and that this process is independent of the Golgi compartment.
the trimeric Go protein-dependent lysosomal pathway is involved in the intracellular trafficking and degradation of N-glycoproteins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the G(i3) proteins are responsible for the intracellular trafficking and degradation of a pool N-glycophosphoproteins in HT-29 cell.
G(i3) is involved in the control of both macroautophagic degradation of a specific pool of N-glycoproteins and their intracellular trafficking.
the lysosomal autophagic pathway is a process that is not dependent upon a secretory pathway, but rather is a process that occurs independently from the Golgi apparatus.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the G(i3) subunit is involved in two different membrane flow processes: (i) macroautophagic trafficking of N-linked proteins from the cytoplasm to lysosomes and (ii) exocytotic trafficking of N-linked glycans from the endoplasmic reticulum to the cell surface.
G(i3) controls the intracellular trafficking and the macroautophagy of N-glycoproteins in HT-29 colon cancer cells.
macroautophagy and exocytosis are two distinct membrane flow processes that can be regulated independently by the G alpha(i) subunit of the trimeric guanine nucleotide-binding protein.
